unit.title: Weld using flux cored arc welding process to FCAW

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: A steel frame job calls for gas-shielded FCAW to the AWS code the Centre uses. What must be in hand before production welding starts?
options: A qualified WPS that covers the joints, positions and wire
The machine maker's leaflet with its suggested settings
A note of the settings the last crew used on the job
The wire spool label showing its weight and lot number

questions.stem: The WPS lists E71T-1C wire with 100% carbon dioxide. Today the store has only an argon and CO2 mix. What should the team leader do?
options: Use the mix, since it gives a smoother arc and less spatter
Use the mix, and turn the voltage down by one or two volts
Hold the work until a WPS covering that gas is approved
Use the mix, and write the change on the weld log later

questions.stem: A job needs vertical-up and overhead FCAW on plate. Which wire marking shows the wire is made for all positions?
options: E70T-1C
E71T-1C
E70T-5C

questions.stem: What does a "J" added to a flux-cored wire classification, as in E71T-1M-J, tell the welder?
options: The wire comes wound on a large drum for production line welding
The wire is only for single-pass joints in thin plate
The core has extra iron powder for faster deposition
The weld metal passed an impact test at a colder temperature

questions.stem: A flux-cored wire classification ends in "H4". What does this tell you about the weld metal?
options: Its hydrogen content is tested and kept very low
It is four times harder than plain mild steel weld
It can be used on plate up to 4 mm thick only
It must be heat treated for four hours after welding

questions.stem: Some self-shielded wires are classified for single-pass welds only. Why must they not be used for multi-pass structural joints?
options: They cannot strike an arc on top of an earlier pass
Their slag is too thin to protect a second pass
Their weld metal may crack or lose toughness in many passes
They give too little penetration to fuse into the root

questions.stem: How does a metal-cored wire, such as one marked E70C-6M, differ from a gas-shielded flux-cored wire?
options: It needs no shielding gas because the metal shields it
It is a solid wire with a thin copper coat on its outside surface
It can only be used on DC electrode negative polarity
Its core is mostly metal powder, so it leaves little slag

questions.stem: Why can it be a problem to run a wire classified only for CO2 with an argon-rich mixed gas?
options: The arc becomes too cold to melt the wire properly
More alloy reaches the weld, which may become too hard
The mixed gas reacts with the flux and makes the fume toxic to breathe
The wire feeds too fast and buries itself in the pool

questions.stem: A set is rated 300 A at 60% duty cycle. The job needs 250 A. Compared with 6 minutes in every 10 at 300 A, how long can it weld at 250 A?
options: Longer, because the current is below the rated value
Shorter, because flux-cored wire draws extra current
The same, because the duty cycle never changes at all
Only 2.5 minutes, because the current has been lowered

questions.stem: To check the wire feed speed, a welder runs wire out for 6 seconds and measures 1.2 m. What is the wire feed speed?
options: 7.2 m/min
12 m/min
1.2 m/min
20 m/min

questions.stem: The contact tip-to-work distance (CTWD) is made 10 mm longer, with the same machine settings. What happens to the welding current?
options: It rises, so the weld penetrates more deeply
It stays the same, as the machine holds it steady
It falls, so the weld penetrates less deeply
It doubles, because more wire is being heated

questions.stem: A pass is run at 26 V, 220 A and 300 mm/min. Using heat input = V × A × 60 ÷ (travel speed × 1000), what is the heat input?
options: 0.87 kJ/mm
1.14 kJ/mm
1.43 kJ/mm
11.4 kJ/mm

questions.stem: Why does a rutile-type gas-shielded wire, such as E71T-1C, suit vertical-up welding?
options: It needs no gas, so the pool cannot be blown away
Its arc is cooler, so the plate does not get hot
It makes no slag, so nothing runs down the joint
Its slag freezes fast and helps hold the pool up

questions.stem: Why do most structural FCAW procedures not allow vertical-down welding on thick plate groove joints?
options: The pool runs ahead and fusion with the plate is poor
The slag cannot be chipped off a vertical-down weld
Vertical-down uses far too much wire for thick plate
The gas cannot reach the arc when welding downward

questions.stem: In the overhead position (4G), a flux-cored cap sags and rolls over at its edges. Which change helps most?
options: A wider weave with a longer pause at the centre
More voltage, so the pool stays fluid for longer
Narrow stringer beads with a little less wire speed
A longer stick-out with a steeper drag angle

questions.stem: A one-sided FCAW butt joint has no steel backing bar. What can be used under the root to support it, if the WPS allows?
options: A strip of hardwood timber clamped tight against the root
A layer of loose flux packed under the joint
An aluminium bar wrapped in wet cloth to cool it
Ceramic backing tape held firmly against the root

questions.stem: On a 3G test plate with a steel backing strip, why must the strip sit tight against both plates?
options: So the plates cannot be bent during the bend test
A gap traps slag and leaves lack of fusion at the root
So less weld metal is needed to fill the groove
A loose strip lets the shielding gas escape upward out of the joint

questions.stem: A WPS for a 10 mm 3G test on backing gives a 6 mm root opening. The fitter sets 3 mm. What is the most likely result?
options: Poor fusion into the root and the backing strip
Burn-through, because the gap is now too narrow
More undercut at the cap, but a sound root pass
A faster weld with no change to the root quality

questions.stem: On a structural steel FCAW job, why does the WPS limit how hot the joint may get between passes?
options: So the welder's gloves do not burn through
So the slag stays soft and is easy to chip off
Too much heat can lower the weld's toughness
So the wire does not melt inside the contact tip

questions.stem: Why may a WPS ask for preheat on 40 mm plate even in Jamaica's hot weather?
options: So the shielding gas flows more evenly out of the nozzle cup
So the flux inside the wire melts before the steel
So the plate does not rust between the weld passes
Thick plate draws heat away and the joint cools fast

questions.stem: A spool of flux-cored wire left on a machine in the open yard for two weeks shows rust spots. What should be done?
options: Take it off and set it aside or scrap it, as the maker says
Wipe the rust off with a rag and carry on welding
Turn the voltage up to burn off the rust as it feeds
Use it for tack welds only and keep it for later

questions.stem: A 1.2 mm flux-cored wire is fed through a gun liner made for 0.8 mm wire. What is the most likely result?
options: Smoother feeding, because the wire is held more tightly
The wire drags and feeds unevenly, or jams in the liner
Nothing changes, because the liner size does not matter
Better gas cover, because the liner seals the gun

questions.stem: The WPS gives 24–28 V. The set's dial reads 26 V, but a meter at the arc reads 23 V. What is a likely cause?
options: The wire is the wrong classification for the job
The gas flow is set too high at the regulator
Voltage lost in long cables or poor connections
The plate is too thick for the dial to read right

questions.stem: A welder passes FCAW groove tests in the 3G and 4G positions on plate. Generally, what does this qualify him for?
options: Flat and horizontal plate welds only, not vertical
Pipe in all positions, but no plate work at all
Vertical and overhead plate only, not flat welds
Plate groove and fillet welds in all positions

questions.stem: Why are bend test strips cut from the middle of an FCAW test plate, and not from its ends?
options: The ends hold the starts and stops, which are discarded
The middle is thicker, so the strips bend more easily
The ends are kept for the welder to take home
The middle cools faster, so it is harder to bend

questions.stem: Before a bend test, why are the cap and the backing strip ground flush on each strip?
options: So the strip fits into a smaller bending jig
So the strip bends evenly and the weld is tested
So the strip looks good in the photo record
So the strip can be weighed against the plate

questions.stem: Why are the long edges of a bend test strip rounded off before it is bent?
options: So the strip slides out of the jig after bending
So the welder's name can be stamped on the edge
Sharp edges can start a crack the weld did not cause
So the bend can be made by hand without a jig

questions.stem: A fillet weld from a 4F FCAW test is cut, polished and etched. What does the etched section show?
options: The welder's speed and the voltage used for each pass
The chemical make-up of the wire and the plate
The hardness of the weld cap at each point
The fusion, root penetration and leg sizes of the weld

questions.stem: On a 3G FCAW joint, slag lines are found along the toes between fill passes. What is the most likely cause?
options: The gas flow was too high for the cup size used
Humped passes left deep valleys at the toes
The plate was preheated to the WPS temperature
The wire was stored sealed in its plastic bag

questions.stem: Porosity is found only at the start of each FCAW run. The gas pre-flow is set to zero. Which fix is most likely to work?
options: Set a short gas pre-flow before the arc starts
Turn the wire speed up at the start of each run
Use a longer stick-out when striking the arc
Raise the voltage for the whole of every run

questions.stem: A bend strip from an FCAW test opens along the bevel face, showing a smooth, shiny surface. What fault does this show?
options: Porosity from damp wire
Undercut at the cap toe
Lack of sidewall fusion
Hydrogen cracking in the HAZ

questions.stem: A deep, narrow FCAW root pass has a crack along its centre line. What is a likely cause?
options: Travel that was too slow for the wire speed
A gas mix that was too rich in argon
Too short a stick-out for the wire diameter
A bead too deep for its width, from high current

questions.stem: Why must the suction on a fume-extraction gun be set carefully for gas-shielded FCAW?
options: Strong suction makes the wire feed too quickly
Too much suction can pull the shielding gas away
Weak suction makes the slag harder to remove
Strong suction cools the plate and causes cracks

questions.stem: Overhead FCAW (4G) drops hot slag and spatter. Which extra protection matters most for the welder?
options: A flame-resistant cap, closed collar and done-up sleeves
A lighter filter shade so the pool can be seen better
Thin cotton gloves for a better feel on the trigger
Short sleeves, so heat can escape from the arms

questions.stem: Several FCAW sets share one steel workbench. Why must each work lead be clamped close to its own joint?
options: So the sets can share one wire feeder between them
So the voltage on the dial reads a little higher than normal
So the welders can work without wearing gloves
So welding current does not stray through other paths

questions.stem: Why can a CO2 regulator freeze up during long FCAW runs at a high flow?
options: CO2 reacts with the brass and forms ice inside
Humid air condenses on the valve and soaks it
The gas cools sharply as it expands in the regulator
The wire feeder draws cold air back into the hose

questions.stem: A gas-shielded flux-cored wire gives about 85% of its weight as weld metal. A job needs 6.8 kg of weld metal. About how much wire is needed?
options: 5.8 kg
7.8 kg
8.0 kg
9.4 kg

questions.stem: A 6 m FCAW fillet weld needs 3 passes at a travel speed of 300 mm/min. What is the total arc time?
options: 20 minutes
45 minutes
60 minutes
180 minutes

questions.stem: Long FCAW fillets are needed on the stiffeners of a steel beam. Which sequence keeps distortion lowest?
options: Short runs balanced on each side, from the centre out
One long run on one side, then one on the other side
Weld from one end to the other in a single pass
Weld the largest welds first, then the small ones

questions.stem: Which visual finding on a 3G FCAW test cap should stop the test before the plate goes for bending?
options: Even ripples with a small cap height above the plate
A crack, or lack of fusion showing at the surface
Light spatter beside the weld that brushes away
A slight colour change in the plate beside the weld

questions.stem: A welder on your crew sets his own voltage and wire speed, outside the WPS range, because the welds "look nicer". What should you do?
options: Let him carry on, as long as the welds look good
Note it down and raise it at next month's meeting
Change the WPS so that it matches his own settings from now on
Stop him, reset to the WPS and check what he welded

questions.stem: Why should the wire classification, lot number and gas be recorded on the weld log for each joint?
options: So a later fault can be traced back to the batch used
So the store knows when to order wire for next month
So the welder's wages can be worked out from it
So the machine's warranty can be claimed later on

questions.stem: You are planning FCAW of 20 column base plates for a warehouse in Portmore. How should the work be set up to raise output and quality?
options: Weld every joint in the position the parts were stacked
Use a positioner so most welds are flat or horizontal
Weld each base plate overhead to train the welders
Use vertical-down on every joint to save arc time

questions.stem: On an exposed site the WPS allows a self-shielded flux-cored wire. Why must the stick-out still be kept as the wire maker says?
options: Too long a stick-out lets the sea breeze blow the wire sideways
A short stick-out makes the wire too stiff to feed
Too short a stick-out can cause porosity with this wire
The stick-out sets the polarity of the welding set

questions.stem: Why should the tack welds on an FCAW test plate be made with the same wire and to the same WPS as the main weld?
options: So the plate is easier to bend in the vice afterwards
So the welder can practise his speed before the test
So the tacks can be left out of the final visual inspection report
Tacks become part of the weld, so they must be as sound

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: In FCAW set-up, what do the letters CTWD stand for?
accepted: the contact tip to work distance

shortAnswers.stem: A plate groove test is welded from underneath, with the plates held flat above the welder. What is its AWS position code?
A welder runs flux-cored wire out of the gun for 6 seconds and measures 0.9 m. What is the wire feed speed, in metres per minute?
In the wire classification E71T-1M, which letter shows the wire is classified for a mixed argon and CO2 gas?
What is the name of the steel strip fixed under the root of a butt joint so that the root can be welded from one side?
A pass is run at 25 V and 200 A at 250 mm/min. Using V × A × 60 ÷ (travel speed × 1000), what is the heat input in kJ/mm?
What is the name of the tubular wire filled mainly with metal powder, which leaves only small islands of slag?
What is the name of the test in which a strip cut across a welded test plate is bent round a former to open up any defects?
What is the name of the short flow of shielding gas that starts before the arc is struck?
What material are the small backing tiles made of that are taped under a one-sided root to support it?
A welding set is rated at 40% duty cycle on a 10-minute cycle. How many minutes in each 10 can it weld at its rated current?
Name the copper part at the end of the FCAW gun that passes the welding current into the wire.
In a wire classification such as E71T-1M H8, what does the letter H stand for?
A flux-cored wire gives 85% of its weight as weld metal. How many kilograms of weld metal will 20 kg of wire give?
What is the AWS position code for a fillet weld on plate in which the weld axis runs straight up and down?

essays.stem: A firm must weld the steel frame of a two-storey building: part in the shop and part on an open site near the sea in St Mary. Compare gas-shielded flux-cored, self-shielded flux-cored and metal-cored wire, and recommend which to use in the shop and which on site.
essays.modelAnswer: Gas-shielded flux-cored wire, such as E71T-1C or 1M, gives a smooth arc, good all-position welds and tough weld metal, but the gas can be blown away by wind, so it suits the shop. Metal-cored wire also needs gas. It leaves very little slag and gives high deposition, so it is good for long flat and horizontal shop welds where cleaning time matters, though it is less easy out of position. Self-shielded flux-cored wire makes its own shielding from the core, so it carries no cylinder and resists wind better, which suits site work near the sea. Its fume is heavier and it needs careful control of stick-out, and only multi-pass grades may be used on structural joints. I would use gas-shielded flux-cored wire for the shop, with metal-cored on long flat runs, and a multi-pass self-shielded wire on site, each covered by its own qualified WPS.
markingPoints: Gas-shielded flux-cored: smooth all-position welds, tough weld metal, but needs shelter from wind
Metal-cored: little slag, high deposition, best on flat and horizontal shop welds; needs gas
Self-shielded: no gas, better in wind, more fume, stick-out critical, multi-pass grade only for structure
Clear recommendation: gas-shielded (and metal-cored) in the shop, self-shielded on site
Each choice must be covered by a qualified WPS

essays.stem: Describe how you would weld a single-V butt test plate in 10 mm steel in the vertical position (3G) with gas-shielded flux-cored wire on a backing strip, from fit-up to cap, following the WPS.
essays.modelAnswer: First I read the WPS and check the wire, gas, polarity, current range, root opening and bevel angle. I clean the bevels and backing strip to bright metal, set the plates on the strip with the root opening the WPS gives, about 6 mm, and tack on the ends of the backing so it sits tight with no gap. I check the gas flow, wire speed and voltage on a scrap plate. I weld uphill. The root pass fuses both bevel faces into the backing, with a slight side-to-side motion and a short pause at each side. I chip and brush all slag, and grind any humps. The fill passes use a slight weave or a shelf motion, pausing at the toes to fill them and avoid slag traps, keeping within the interpass limit. The cap is laid flat, about 1–3 mm proud, overlapping each edge by about 1.5 mm. I then clean it and check it visually before it goes for bend tests.
markingPoints: Reads the WPS and checks wire, gas, polarity, settings, root opening and bevel
Cleans bevels and backing; tacks so the backing is tight with the right opening
Welds uphill; root fuses both bevels into the backing
Cleans slag fully between passes; pauses at the toes on fill passes; keeps interpass limit
Flat cap of correct height and overlap; visual check before testing

essays.stem: Explain what the main variables on an FCAW welding procedure specification (WPS) are, why each one is controlled, and what must happen if one has to change on a job.
essays.modelAnswer: A WPS for FCAW sets the base metal and thickness range, the joint design (bevel, root opening, backing), the wire classification and diameter, the shielding gas and flow, the polarity, the current or wire speed range, the voltage range, the travel speed, the stick-out, the positions and direction (for example vertical-up), the preheat and interpass temperatures, and the number of passes. Each one changes how the weld fuses and how strong and tough the weld metal is. A different gas or wire can change the weld chemistry. Higher heat input can lower toughness. A different joint or position can leave lack of fusion. If one of these must change, the welder must not just carry on. The team leader checks whether the change is within the WPS range. If it is not, the work stops until a WPS that covers it is found or is qualified and approved, and the welders are briefed on it.
markingPoints: Lists the main variables: material, joint, wire, gas, polarity, current/voltage/speed, stick-out, position, preheat/interpass
Explains that they control fusion, strength and toughness of the weld
Gives at least one example of how a change spoils the weld (gas, heat input, position)
Change outside the range: stop, get a covering or newly qualified WPS approved
Welders briefed and records updated

essays.stem: Explain how a welder's FCAW plate qualification test in the 3G and 4G positions is usually carried out and judged under the AWS code the Centre uses.
essays.modelAnswer: The test plates are cut and bevelled to the test drawing and fitted on a backing strip with the root opening the WPS gives. The assessor marks the plates with the welder's identity so they cannot be swapped. The welder sets up to the WPS and welds one plate vertical-up (3G) and one overhead (4G) without moving the plates out of position, cleaning between passes. The finished caps are checked visually: no cracks, no lack of fusion, undercut and cap height within the code's limits. If the visual check passes, strips are cut from set places, away from the ends, the backing and cap are ground flush and the edges rounded. Usually a face and a root bend, or side bends on thick plate, are bent round a former. The bent strips are judged against the code's limit for open defects. Passing both positions generally qualifies the welder for plate in all positions, and the result is written on a qualification record.
markingPoints: Plates prepared to the test drawing and WPS, and marked so they cannot be swapped
Welded in fixed 3G and 4G positions to the WPS
Visual inspection first, against the code's limits
Bend strips cut from set places, prepared, bent and judged against the code's limit
Result recorded; 3G plus 4G generally qualifies all positions on plate

essays.stem: Describe the technique for overhead FCAW (4G and 4F), and explain how a welder avoids the defects that are common in that position.
essays.modelAnswer: Overhead, gravity pulls the pool down, so the welder keeps it small. The current and wire speed are set at the lower end of the WPS range, and narrow stringer beads are used instead of a wide weave. The gun is held with a slight drag angle and the work angle set so the pool wets both sides. The welder moves at a steady speed so the slag freezes behind the pool and supports it. Sagging and a rolled-over cap come from too large a pool or too slow travel, and are cured with smaller beads and faster travel. Slag traps at the toes are avoided by keeping each bead flat and cleaning well between passes. Undercut comes from too much heat or a wrong angle. The welder takes a comfortable, braced stance, with a flame-resistant cap, closed collar and done-up sleeves to keep falling slag and spatter off the skin.
markingPoints: Small pool: lower settings in the WPS range, narrow stringer beads
Correct gun and work angles and steady travel so the slag supports the pool
Sagging/rolled cap: cause and cure
Slag traps and undercut: cause and cure; clean between passes
Body position and PPE against falling slag and spatter

essays.stem: Explain how you would set and check the parameters on an FCAW set before a job to a WPS: wire feed speed, voltage at the arc, stick-out and gas flow. Show how you would work out the heat input of a pass.
essays.modelAnswer: I set the polarity for the wire, then the wire feed speed and voltage in the WPS range. To check the wire speed I release the drive pressure from the weld, run wire for 6 seconds, measure it and multiply by 10 to get metres per minute. I check the voltage with a meter at the gun and the work, not only on the dial, because long cables lose volts. I set the contact tip-to-work distance the wire maker gives and keep it steady, because a longer stick-out lowers the current. I set the gas flow with a flowmeter at the gun. I make a test bead on scrap, then record the readings. Heat input is volts × amps × 60 ÷ (travel speed in mm/min × 1000). For example, 26 V and 220 A at 300 mm/min gives 26 × 220 × 60 ÷ 300 000 = 1.14 kJ/mm, which I compare with the WPS limit.
markingPoints: Wire feed speed measured (timed run-out, scaled to m/min)
Voltage checked at the arc with a meter, not only the dial
Stick-out set to the maker's figure and its effect on current explained
Gas flow checked and test bead made; readings recorded
Heat input formula used correctly with a worked example

essays.stem: Explain the causes of porosity, slag inclusions, lack of sidewall fusion and centreline cracking in FCAW, and how each one can be prevented.
essays.modelAnswer: Porosity is gas trapped in the weld. It comes from lost gas cover (wind, no pre-flow, blocked nozzle, leaks), damp or rusty wire, dirty plate or the wrong stick-out. It is prevented by sheltering the joint, setting pre-flow, keeping nozzles clean, storing wire dry and cleaning the plate. Slag inclusions come from slag left between passes or from humped beads that leave valleys at the toes. They are prevented by chipping and brushing every pass, grinding humps and pausing at the toes. Lack of sidewall fusion comes from low heat, fast travel, a wrong gun angle or too narrow a groove. It is prevented by settings within the WPS, aiming at the bevel faces and keeping the joint design right. Centreline cracking comes from a bead that is deep and narrow, often from high current in a tight groove, or high restraint. It is prevented by keeping the bead wider than it is deep, using the right groove angle and following any preheat.
markingPoints: Porosity: causes (gas cover, damp wire, dirt, stick-out) and prevention
Slag inclusions: causes (poor cleaning, humped beads) and prevention
Lack of sidewall fusion: causes (low heat, fast travel, angle, narrow groove) and prevention
Centreline cracking: deep narrow bead or restraint, and prevention
Prevention linked to following the WPS

essays.stem: As the person in charge of an FCAW production bay, explain the main hazards of all-position flux-cored welding and the controls you would put in place.
essays.modelAnswer: FCAW makes heavy fume, which can contain manganese, so I would fit extraction at the arc or fume-extraction guns, set so they do not pull the gas away, and give respirators where extraction is not enough. Arc light needs screens and the right filter shade. Overhead and vertical welding drop hot slag and spatter, so welders wear flame-resistant jackets, caps and done-up collars and sleeves, and the area is cleared of anything that burns, with an extinguisher close by. Electric shock is controlled by checking cables and guns, dry gloves and work leads clamped close to the joint. Gas cylinders are chained upright, with regulators checked. Wire spools are heavy, so they are lifted correctly. Hot work is marked hot. I would brief the team on these points, check them daily and follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules.
markingPoints: Fume: extraction at the arc (not disturbing gas), respirators where needed
Arc light and burns: screens, shade, flame-resistant clothing, cap and closed collar for overhead work
Fire: clear combustibles, extinguisher, hot work marked
Electrical: cable checks, dry gloves, work lead close to the joint
Cylinders and manual handling; briefing and daily checks

essays.stem: You lead three welders on an FCAW job to weld 12 portal frame knee joints for a warehouse in Portmore to an AWS code. Explain how you would plan, run and check the work.
essays.modelAnswer: Before starting I read the drawings, the weld symbols and the code requirements, and get the approved WPS for each joint. I check that each welder holds a qualification that covers the process, positions and thickness, and allocate joints to match. I check that the wire classification, lot and gas match the WPS, and that wire is stored dry. I plan the welding sequence to control distortion and use a positioner where I can, so most welds are flat or horizontal. I brief the team on the WPS, the sequence, safety and the hold points. The first knee joint is inspected before the rest go ahead. During the work I check settings, preheat if required, interpass, cleaning and fit-up. Each weld is numbered on a weld map with the welder, wire lot and inspection result. Any fault is recorded, repaired to procedure and re-inspected before handover.
markingPoints: Reads drawings and code; gets the approved WPS for each joint
Checks welder qualifications and allocates joints to match
Checks consumables and plans the sequence and positioning
Briefs the team; first-off inspection and checks during work
Weld map and records; faults repaired and re-inspected

essays.stem: Explain why multi-pass FCAW on thick plate causes distortion and how you would control and check it on a welded beam or frame.
essays.modelAnswer: Each FCAW pass heats the steel, which expands, and the weld metal shrinks as it cools. Many passes on one side of a joint pull it out of line, causing angular distortion, bowing or twisting. FCAW lays down a lot of metal quickly, so the shrinkage can be large. To control it I would avoid over-welding beyond the size on the drawing, use a double-V or balanced joint where the design allows, and weld alternately on each side. I would tack and clamp the parts firmly, or use strongbacks, and preset the parts so they pull back to line. Back-step or skip sequences spread the heat. Keeping to the WPS heat input also helps. I would check straightness and squareness with a straight edge, string line, square and diagonals at set stages, and record the readings so the sequence can be changed before the work goes too far.
markingPoints: Explains expansion and shrinkage; FCAW deposits a lot of metal
Do not over-weld; balanced joints and alternate sides
Clamping, strongbacks and presetting
Back-step or skip sequences and heat input control
Checks at stages (straight edge, string line, diagonals) and records

practical1.title: FCAW single-V butt test plates in the vertical (3G) position on a backing strip, with bend tests
practical1.brief: Your group is given an FCAW WPS for a single-V butt joint in 10 mm carbon steel plate on a backing strip, welded vertical-up (3G). Together, read the WPS and write a short plan: the settings, the order in which members weld, and who checks what. Then each member prepares, fits and tacks one test plate on its backing strip, sets the wire speed, voltage, stick-out and gas flow to the WPS, checks the wire speed by a timed run-out, and welds the root, fill and cap passes vertical-up, cleaning between passes. While one member welds, another records the settings and interpass checks on the weld log. When the plates are cool, each member visually inspects another member's plate and records the result. Where the Centre has a bend jig, the assessor cuts two strips from each passed plate and the group prepares and bends them; otherwise the strips are prepared and kept for the assessor to bend. Photograph each stage and hand in the plan, the weld log and the inspection sheets.
materials: An FCAW WPS for a 10 mm single-V butt on backing, 3G (from the assessor)
Pairs of 10 mm carbon steel plates bevelled to the WPS, with backing strips
Gas-shielded flux-cored wire to the WPS (for example 1.2 mm E71T-1C or 1M) and the matching gas
FCAW set with a flowmeter, and a voltmeter or the set's arc display
Stopwatch and tape measure for the wire speed check
Grinder, chipping hammer, wire brush, weld gauges and temperature crayons
Weld log and visual inspection sheets
Bend jig, if the Centre has one
photos: The group's plan and the WPS settings written on the weld log
A test plate tacked on its backing strip, with the root opening being measured
The timed wire run-out being measured
The root pass, cleaned, on one plate
A finished cap on each plate, with the plate's mark visible
Bend strips after bending, or prepared strips ready for the assessor
checklist: Read the WPS and set wire speed, voltage, stick-out and gas within its ranges
Checked wire speed by a timed run-out and recorded the result
Fitted and tacked the plate on the backing with the correct root opening and no gap under the root
Welded vertical-up with sound fusion, cleaning slag fully between passes
Kept within the interpass limit and recorded settings on the weld log
Finished cap: even, within cap height limits, no cracks, undercut within limits
Inspected another member's plate and recorded the result accurately
Worked safely and left the bay clean, with wire and offcuts stored
safety: Use fume extraction at the arc and keep your head out of the plume
Wear full PPE, with a flame-resistant cap and closed collar for vertical work
Chain gas cylinders upright and check hoses before use
Treat plates and strips as hot: use tongs and mark hot work
Bend tests only with the jig's guards in place and the assessor present

practical2.title: FCAW fillet welds in the vertical-up (3F) and overhead (4F) positions, with fillet break and macro checks
practical2.brief: As a group, weld tee-joint fillet test pieces in 10 mm carbon steel plate in the vertical-up (3F) and overhead (4F) positions with gas-shielded flux-cored wire, to a fillet weld WPS from the assessor. First, together, plan the job: the settings from the WPS, the order of welding, the leg size asked for, and who records and who inspects. Each member welds at least one 3F and one 4F fillet, about 200 mm long, while another member records the settings, the arc time and the travel speed. Measure each weld's legs with a fillet gauge. Then, under the assessor's direction, break one test piece of each position by bending the upright plate over the weld (fillet break test), and saw a cross-section from another piece for a macro check: the group files, sands and etches it with the etchant the Centre approves. Each member writes up one result. Photograph each stage and hand in the weld log and a short test report.
materials: Fillet weld WPS for 3F and 4F (from the assessor)
Tee-joint pieces in 10 mm carbon steel plate, about 200 mm long
Gas-shielded flux-cored wire and gas to the WPS
FCAW set with positioning stand for vertical and overhead work
Fillet weld gauge, stopwatch and steel rule
Press or large vice and hammer for the break test
Bandsaw, files, abrasive paper and an approved etchant with its SDS
Weld log and test report forms
photos: The tee pieces set up in the 3F and 4F positions
A member welding overhead in full PPE
Finished 3F and 4F fillets with the fillet gauge on the legs
A broken fillet showing the fracture face
The completed weld log and test report
checklist: Set the FCAW parameters to the WPS and recorded them
Welded a 3F fillet vertical-up with even legs and no undercut beyond the limit
Welded a 4F fillet overhead with small, even beads and no sag
Measured leg sizes correctly with the fillet gauge
Took part safely in the fillet break or macro preparation
Read the fracture face or macro correctly: root fusion, porosity, leg size
Recorded results clearly and accurately on the report
safety: Wear a flame-resistant cap, closed collar and done-up sleeves when welding overhead
Use fume extraction at the arc
Wear eye protection when breaking test pieces, and keep others clear
Handle the etchant with gloves and goggles as the SDS says, in a ventilated place
Mark hot work and use tongs
